en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
The work titled *Nītipatha*, adorned with the commentary named *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages.
The second chapter:
The Declaration of the Chapter’s Subject Matter; how the suspicion that [the scripture] does not touch upon the actual meaning is refuted, as in the case of verbal expression.
Likewise, an effort is being made by the disciples of the teacher Prabhākara. // 1 //
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): Here, some disputants, due to the misconception that worldly sentences are subject to deviation, assert that speech does not touch upon its object. (2)

The ascertainment of an object is its contact [with cognition], and that belongs only to perception and the like which do not deviate from the object; verbal testimony, however, is subject to deviation.
For even without an external object, cognition arises through words, as in such expressions as, "There is a herd of elephants on the tip of a finger. (4)
Nor can it be argued here that this is an error due to non-apprehension— like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl— because there is no distinction in the cause.
For defective causes are incapable of producing a complete effect;
therefore, it is logical to perceive a distinction [between the cause and its result] in cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver.
But here, the word which is the cause of knowledge is not distinguished;
whereas that which is distinguished is the speaker, and he is not the cause of the knowledge.
If the speaker were also a cause for cognition, like the sense organs and so forth, then there would likewise be non-apprehension of it due to his own defect. (8)
The speaker, however, is employed solely for the manifestation of the word;
knowledge, on the other hand, is produced by the word alone, independently [of the speaker]. (9)
And no defect whatsoever is perceived in it here;
moreover, a defect is the cause for non-perception, so in its absence, perception is evident. (10)
Therefore, this very cognition produced by the word transcends the object in such a manner; how, then, can there be certainty regarding the object on its basis? // 11 //
"For that which exists is established even without [the presence of] another; certainty regarding it arises through that [other]"—this is a well-spoken statement. (12)
But if this is so, how can practical activity arise from the words of authoritative persons?
For how could there be worldly activity for people without certainty? (13)
It is said that worldly convention indeed proceeds even from doubt; it is commonly observed, and because of that, nothing here is corrupted. (14)

Moreover, having considered the reliability of the speaker, the ascertainment of the meaning therein can also be established in some way through the force of another means of valid cognition (māna). // 15 //
"Alas! The Veda, because its subject matter is supersensible and because it lacks an author, has indeed been brought to a wretched state by the learned! (16)
The established conclusion:
here, those possessed of intelligence strive to provide a rebuttal; the fallibility of cognition has been refuted in the *Nayavīthī*. (17)
Listen with attention to the nature of even human speech;
the wise do not maintain that it is distinct from inference. (18)
For worldly speech, whose composition always depends upon persons, is inherently suspect of being untrue; thus, it does not by itself determine the actual meaning.
For even men are seen composing words whose meanings are not mutually connected; therefore, there is no certainty regarding syntactic connection.
Some [err] merely through delusion, some due to a defect in their intention, some through negligence, some through incapacity, and some because they propound incoherent arguments. (21)
Although the word-meanings expressed by those [words] possess the fitness for syntactic connection,
nevertheless, because even that which is unconnected is observed, there is no certainty regarding their connection.

In this context, by the word "ascertainment" (niścaya), knowledge itself is denoted; therefore, when there is no ascertainment of positive concomitance (anvaya), there is only knowledge regarding that [concomitance], but no actual positive concomitance. (23)
Therefore, a human statement whose composition is suspected of being untrue does not, merely upon being heard, bring about certainty regarding its object. (24)
As long as there is another preceding means of valid cognition, not yet known by the speaker, which has the intended object as its domain and is based on the sense organs and their objects. (25)
His knowledge is understood through his speech acting as a logical mark (liṅga);
for it is determined that he speaks only after having known the meaning. (26)
His speech is invariably accompanied by knowledge and thus serves as an indicator of that knowledge;
and since knowledge is inseparable from the object, there is consequently certainty regarding the object itself. // 27 //
Once that object has been ascertained therein, that object is subsequently understood through the sentence;
at that stage, that sentence would possess the character of a restatement (anuvāda). (28)
Previously, however, that [word] was considered a mark for ascertaining the speaker's knowledge;
for a sentence is held to be the effect produced by the speaker's knowledge. (29)
Furthermore, for everyone, the establishment of a cause from an effect occurs through inference;
therefore, a statement composed by a person is not designated as a scripture.

And this being the case, while this deviation is observed in the indicative mark (liṅga), it is not so for the scripture; how then could that [scripture] fail to touch upon its actual meaning? // 31 //
Nor is there any such deviation in the case of the logical mark (liṅga); however, it is the dull-witted person who is unable to distinguish between what is a valid mark and what is not.
In that case, because of the commonality of form with the linga, this erroneous conventional usage of the term "linga" occurs with respect to what is not a linga. (33)
This has been explained in detail in the section on *śruti* and *liṅga*;
therefore, there is no deviation between these two types of scriptural authority based on indicative marks (*liṅga*). (34)
But surely the object itself is first understood from the sentences of a person; for otherwise, how could the speaker’s specific cognition be inferred? (35)
For the distinction between cognitions occurs solely through their objects, since cognitions themselves lack form;
and a distinction cannot be conceived by means of an object that is not perceived.
To this we reply: due to the suspicion that it may not correspond to reality, the object is not ascertained; and since it is not ascertained, it is not known—this much is established. (37)
However, even when the meaning of the sentence is not yet known, once the collection of words has been heard, such an inquiry arises in the mind of a discerning listener: (38)
This person utters a collection of words whose meanings are capable of mutual connection; therefore, it is certain that this authoritative person (āpta) has indeed understood their coherence. (39)
He never intends to speak of things that are unrelated, nor of those whose connection is not recognized; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. (40)
Surely, having thus mounted the horse, you have forgotten the horse itself;
having set out for the sake of establishing the authority of the Vedas, you have now abandoned them.

For a word whose power is understood from common worldly usage is the means of cognition in the Veda; and you yourself have accepted that in the world, cognition arises through the state of being a logical mark (liṅga). (42)
However, the Teacher himself has demonstrated the resolution here, while showing that there is a relationship between a word and its meaning. (43)
For when it is established that words denote their meanings as already connected, the specific cognition of the speaker can be known; otherwise, it cannot be. (44)
For it has been demonstrated that when objects are known, the listener would otherwise not conceive of the mutual connection [of words] in the speaker; it is not possible otherwise. (45)
The capacity of words for their respective word-meanings exists naturally; it is merely obscured in the case of human utterances due to the suspicion of error. (46)
But regarding the Vedas, which have no remembered author, which [exist] in their own form, and which bring about the comprehension of objects untouched by other means of knowledge— (47)

There can be no inference of an author on the basis of the mark of "being a sentence," because an author would not be able to compose a sentence concerning a matter that is beyond worldly experience. (48)
Therefore, there is no possibility whatsoever of doubt regarding contradiction with the Veda;
because it is the cause for the ascertainment of meaning, its contact with the object is established. (49)
This path of reasoning, cleared of the mud of verbal impurities and having the thorns of opposing arguments uprooted, has been fashioned by Śālikanātha with even greater rectitude. (50)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Path of Policy" (*nītipatha*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the venerable Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra. // 2 //
